{{Short description|Product of two categories, in category theory}}
{{Redirect|Product of categories|the operation on objects of a category|Product (category theory)}}

In the [[Mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[category theory]], the '''product''' of two [[Category (mathematics)|categories]] ''C'' and ''D'', denoted {{nowrap| ''C'' × ''D''}} and called a '''product category''', is an extension of the concept of the [[Cartesian product]] of two [[Set (mathematics)|sets]]. Product categories are used to define [[Functor#Bifunctors and multifunctors|bifunctors and multifunctors]].{{sfn|Mac Lane|1978|p=37}}

==Definition==
The product category {{nowrap| ''C'' × ''D''}} has:
*as [[Object (category theory)|objects]]:
*:pairs of objects {{nowrap| (''A'', ''B'')}}, where ''A'' is an object of ''C'' and ''B'' of ''D'';
*as [[Morphism|arrows]] from {{nowrap| (''A''<sub>1</sub>, ''B''<sub>1</sub>)}} to  {{nowrap| (''A''<sub>2</sub>, ''B''<sub>2</sub>)}}:
*:pairs of arrows {{nowrap| (''f'', ''g'')}}, where {{nowrap| ''f'' : ''A''<sub>1</sub> → ''A''<sub>2</sub>}} is an arrow of ''C'' and {{nowrap| ''g'' : ''B''<sub>1</sub> → ''B''<sub>2</sub>}} is an arrow of ''D'';
*as composition, component-wise composition from the contributing categories:
*:{{nowrap|1= (''f''<sub>2</sub>, ''g''<sub>2</sub>) <small>o</small> (''f''<sub>1</sub>, ''g''<sub>1</sub>) = (''f''<sub>2</sub> <small>o</small> ''f''<sub>1</sub>, ''g''<sub>2</sub> <small>o</small> ''g''<sub>1</sub>)}};
*as identities, pairs of identities from the contributing categories:
*:1<sub>(''A'', ''B'')</sub> = (1<sub>''A''</sub>, 1<sub>''B''</sub>).

A product of a family of categories is defined exactly the same way.

== Universal property ==
Just like for sets, a product of a family of categories is characterized by the following universal property. Given categories <math>C_i</math> indexed by a set <math>I</math>, <math>P = \prod C_i, p_j : P \to C_j, j \in I</math> satisfy:
:given a family of functors <math>f_i : D \to C_i</math>, there exists a unique functor <math>f : D \to P</math> such that <math>f_j = p_j \circ f</math> for each <math>j \in I</math>.

Put in another way, a product of a family of small categories is exactly the [[categorical product]] of them in the category of small categories <math>\mathsf{Cat}</math>. Thus, for example,
<math display=block>\textstyle \mathsf{Fct}(A, \prod_i B_i) \simeq \prod_i \mathsf{Fct}(A, B_i)</math>

where <math>\mathsf{Fct}</math> denotes a [[functor category]].<ref>{{harvnb|Mac Lane|1978|loc=Ch. II., § 5., Exercise 2.}}</ref>

== Functoriality ==
Given two functors <math>f : C \to D, g : C' \to D'</math>, the product <math>f \times g : C \times C' \to D \times D'</math> is defined component-wise; that is,
<math display=block>(f \times g)(x, x') = (f(x), g(x'))</math>
for a pair of objects or morphisms <math>x, x'</math>.<ref name=products>{{harvnb|Mac Lane|1978|loc=Ch. II., § 3.}}</ref> (This product may also be characterized by the universal property similar to that for categories.) This way, we get the functor
:<math>\times : \mathsf{Cat} \times \mathsf{Cat} \to \mathsf{Cat}.</math>
It satisfies the [[tensor-hom adjunction]] in the sense
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Cat}}(A \times B, C) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Cat}}(A, \mathsf{Fct}(B, C))</math>
where <math>\mathsf{Fct}</math> denotes a [[functor category]].<ref>{{harvnb|Mac Lane|1978|loc=Ch. II., § 5., Exercise 1.}}</ref>

== Example: C × 2 ==
Let <math>f, g : C \to D</math> be functors. Suppose there is a natural transformation <math>\varphi : f \to g</math>. Then <math>\varphi</math> determines the functor
:<math>h : C \times \underline{2} \to D</math>
such that
:<math>h(\cdot, 0) = f, \, h(\cdot, 1) = g</math>,
where <math>\underline{2} = \{ 0, 1 \}</math> is the category with two objects and the non-identity morphism <math>\rightsquigarrow: 0 \to 1</math>.<ref name=products /> Intuitively, ''h'' is a non-invertible ''homotopy'' from <math>f</math> to <math>g</math>. Indeed, define <math>h</math> by, for <math>x : a \to b</math> in <math>C</math>,
:<math>h(x, \operatorname{id}_0) = f(x), \, h(x, \operatorname{id}_1) = g(x), \, h(x, \rightsquigarrow) = g(x) \circ \varphi_a = \varphi_b \circ f(x).</math>

Conversely, given <math>h : C \times \underline{2} \to D</math>, we get <math>f, g, \varphi</math> by <math>f = h(\cdot, 0), \, g = h(\cdot, 1)</math> and <math>\varphi_a = h(\operatorname{id}_a, \rightsquigarrow)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Mac Lane|1978|loc=Ch. II., § 4., Exercise 8.}}</ref>

== Bifunctor ==
A [[functor]] whose domain is a product category is called a '''bifunctor'''. A bifunctor can be defined in each variable separately in the following sense:

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Mac Lane|1978|loc=Ch. II., § 3., Proposition 1.}}</ref> Each bifunctor
:<math>F : A \times B \to C</math>
determines the families of the functors, for objects <math>a</math> in <math>A</math> and <math>b</math> in <math>B</math>,
:<math>F_b : A \to C, \, F_a : B \to C</math>
given by
:<math>F_b a = F(a, b)</math> and <math>F_b f = F(f, \operatorname{id}_b)</math>
for <math>f : a \to a'</math> and similarly for <math>F_a</math>. They commute in the sense:
:<math>F_{a'} g \circ F_b f = F_{b'} f \circ F_a g</math>.

Conversely, given families of functors <math>F_b, F_a</math> as above, if they commute, they define the bifunctor <math>F : A \times B \to C</math> by
:<math>F(f, g) = F_{b'} f \circ F_a g</math>.}}

For example, consider <math>(a, b) \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}(a, b) : C^{op} \times C \to \mathsf{Set}</math>. For each fixed <math>b</math> in <math>B</math>, we have the functor
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(-, b) : C^{op} \to \mathsf{Set}</math>
by [[pullback]]; i.e., <math>f : a \to a'</math> goes to the function
:<math>f^* : \operatorname{Hom}(a', b) \to \operatorname{Hom}(a, b)</math>
defined by <math>f^* g = g \circ f</math>. On the other hand, <math>\operatorname{Hom}(a, -) : C \to \mathsf{Set}</math>
is defined by pushforward; i.e., <math>f \mapsto f_* = f \circ -</math>. Clearly, these two functors commute (the associativity of composition) and so, by the proposition, we get the functor called the [[Hom functor]]
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(-, -) : C^{op} \times C \to \mathsf{Set},</math>
which is explicitly given as: <math>(f, g) \mapsto (h \mapsto g \circ h \circ f).</math>

There is a similar result for natural transformations between bifunctors:

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Mac Lane|1978|loc=Ch. II., § 3., Proposition 2.}}</ref> Let <math>F, G : A, B \to C</math> be bifunctors and
:<math>\alpha = \{ \alpha_{a, b} : F(a, b) \to G(a, b) \mid a \in \operatorname{Ob}(A), b \in \operatorname{Ob}(B) \}</math>
a family of morphisms. Then <math>\alpha : F \to G</math> is a natural transformation if and  only if it is natural in the first variable and the second variable separately; i.e., for each object <math>b</math> in <math>B</math>,
:<math>\alpha_{-, b} : F(-, b) \to G(-, b)</math>
is a natural transformation and similarly in the second variable.}}
<!-- already mentioned above ==Generalization to several arguments==
Just as the binary Cartesian product is readily generalized to an [[Cartesian product#n-ary product|''n''-ary Cartesian product]], binary product of two categories can be generalized, completely analogously, to a product of ''n'' categories. The product operation on categories is [[commutative]] and [[associative]], [[up to isomorphism]], and so this generalization brings nothing new from a theoretical point of view.-->
